description: Hermit crab (Dardanus calidus) with 3 sea anemones (Calliactis parasitica) on its back, Cape Palos, Spain. This species of crab can grow to a length of 12 centimetres (4.7 in) and it uses either large gastropod shells, such as those of Tonna galea and Charonia, which it often decorates with one or more sea anemones of the species Calliactis parasitica. The relationship between the sea anemone and the hermit crab is mutualistic: the sea anemone protects the hermit crab with its stings, and benefits from the food thrown up by the hermit crab's movements. Dardanus calidus is a scavenger, feeding on decaying matter from the sea bed. It has been collected from depths greater than 100 metres (330 ft), but is more typically found in shallower water, and it's spread from the East Atlantic (Portugal to Senegal) and Mediterranean Sea.

description:
The hymenopteran Paracodrus apterogynus (Haliday, 1839) is a gregarious parasitoid of click beetle (Elateridae) larvae (wireworms). Females are virtually wingless searching and attacking their hosts in the soil and laying up to 20 eggs in one larva. The young wasp larvae feed on the larva of which only the dried up shell remains. The parasitism level is actually low. Of several thousands wireworms, only 2 to 5 are parasitized. In this image a parasitized larva of the click beetle Agriotes obscurus is demonstrated.
The parasitized wireworm was collected in Estonia on August 27, 2021. 

The parasitized wireworm was photographed on dark background using the digital Canon EOS 5D Mark II camera, Canon MP-E 65mm f/2.8 lens and diffused flash light.

creator: Enno Merivee
usage_terms: Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication
description:
Recently, it was discovered that various insects with seemingly transparent wings, display vivid structural coloration against dark backgrounds. Wavelength of the reflected light is dependent on the thickness of the chitinous membrane of the wing, microstructures (see at high magnification), hair and scale placement, and venation. In some insects (Drosophila sp.), WIPs may function as species- and sex-specific visual mating cues in a range of taxa. The role of species-specific WIPs in Culicidae mosquitoes is unknown.
About 70 small, partial focus stacked images across the mosquito wing were photomicrographed at 50X magnification with the Microscope Nikon Eclipse FN1 and digital camera Nikon DS-Ri2. These small image stacks were merged together using the image processing software Photoshop. 

Image was taken on November 18, 2021. The image is a crop of the very large original image with the resolution of 41632 x 17530 pixels.

creator: Janek Lass
description: Copepods are aquatic animals like most crustaceans. They live en masse in all depths of both sea and fresh water, as well as in puddles, swamps, and some species in moist moss and wasteland. Among them are also parasites whose appearance can be changed beyond recognition and which live on fish and other aquatic animals. Free-living copepods are only a few millimeters long (0,5-2mm) and play an important part in the water body's food chain: they reproduce relatively quickly, and by feeding on tiny microscopic organisms, they themselves are constantly food for larger aquatic animals. Around 8,500 species of copepods are known in the world, according to the latest data, 82 are known in Estonia, but the existence of 100 species is assumed.

creator: Janek Lass
description:
The genus Scapholeberis differs from other daphnids both in its exterior habitués and by its behaviour, however its anatomical details have the same peculiarities which are characteristic for this family. The head bends forward and is almost a continuum of the dorsal edge of the carapace. Quite often the anterior part of the head (forehead) is armoured with an upward turned horn. Sars described this variant as a true species, S. cornuta. Posteriorly the ventral edge of the carapace ends up in a strong spine. Its postabdomen has much in common with the postabomen found in Ceriodaphnia sp. S. mucronata has a dark colour, sometimes almost black. Female length is 0.6–1.4 mm and male length is 0.4–0.8 mm.
This specimen was found in a city pond in the city of Rakvere in Estonia.

creator: Janek Lass
description:
Water mites (Hydracarina) are a very species-rich group of small arachnids, divided into more than 50 genera. There are over 6,000 species in the world, over 100 in Estonia. In Estonia, water mites mostly live in shallow stagnant waters. In other parts of the world, they are also often found in streams, springs, groundwater and the sea. They all come from land-dwelling ancestors. The life cycle consists of a parasitic larva, two pupal-like resting stages (proto- and tritonymph), a predatory deutonymph and a predatory adult. There are four pairs of true legs, the body is spherical or disk-shaped. Larvae parasitize insects, whose larvae they can easily spread to other bodies of water.
This specimen was found in a city pond in the city of Rakvere in Estonia

creator: Janek Lass
description:
A water mite (Hydrachnidia) photographed in lateral view under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected in May 2023. Water mites represent one of the most diverse and abundant groups of aquatic invertebrates. The lateral view particularly emphasizes the characteristic spherical body of water mites, with its translucent surface displaying a beautiful bluish-green iridescence. The limbs with their distinctive spiny bristles are also clearly visible.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which excellently highlights the texture of the semi-transparent body surface and the fine details of the appendages. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly emphasizes the surface structures and metallic sheen of the carapace. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

creator: Janek Lass
description:
A freshwater ostracod of genus Heterocypris (Heterocypris sp.) photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected from a pond in Rakvere, Estonia, in April 2024. The image clearly shows the characteristic bivalved carapace of the ostracod, which is semi-transparent with a greenish-yellow coloration. The fine setae along the edge of the carapace and the characteristic antennae are particularly well visible. The antennae extending from the carapace are important locomotory organs for ostracods.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which excellently highlights the semi-transparent structure of the animal's carapace and its delicate appendages. The lighting technique used differs from conventional transmitted microscope illumination - instead, reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash was used. This lighting solution allows for exceptional detail in revealing the object's surface texture and transparent structures.

The image was created using focus stacking technique, which allows achieving great depth of field even in microscopic photography. This technique is particularly important when photographing microorganisms, as it enables sharp details to be captured in both the near and far portions of the subject.

description:
A freshwater ostracod (Heterocypris incongruens) photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective lens. The specimen was collected from an urban pond in May 2024. The image prominently features the characteristic muscle scar pattern located on the inner surface of the carapace. This pattern consists of clusters of oval marks that represent the attachment points of muscles used to open and close the shell. This trait is species-specific and critical for accurate identification.
Additionally, the semi-transparent greenish-yellow carapace is visible, along with fine setae along the edge, which assist the ostracod in locomotion and anchoring in its environment. The image was captured using reflected light, which highlights the surface texture of the carapace and the muscle scar impressions. A focus stacking technique was employed, ensuring excellent depth of field and sharp detail throughout the entire subject.

creator: Janek Lass
description:
A water flea of genus Daphnia photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected on July 9, 2023. Of particular interest is the dark resting egg or ephippium in the dorsal brood pouch - this is a specialized resistant structure that forms when environmental conditions become unfavorable. The production of resting eggs is a survival strategy of water fleas, allowing them to survive adverse conditions, similar to plant seeds. The transparent body also shows a characteristic reticulated pattern and bluish tints.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which highlights the transparent carapace and the dark resting egg within. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly emphasizes the surface structures. The image was created using focus stacking technique, which ensures great depth of field throughout the subject.

A male water mite (Arrenurus sp.) photographed under a microscope using an 8x objective. The specimen was collected in June 2023. The image clearly shows the characteristic pear-shaped body form of male water mites and their distinctive posterior extension, which is the main feature distinguishing males from females. The body surface displays a characteristic reticulated pattern and red eyes. The appendages are transparent and covered with spiny bristles.
The specimen was photographed against a black background, which creates a strong contrast with the yellowish-brown body surface texture and fine details of the appendages. The lighting technique used was reflected light from a photographic speedlight flash, which particularly emphasizes the surface structures and patterns. creator: Janeklass
description: The image depicts the larva of Cataclysta lemnata, an aquatic species that lives entirely underwater and constructs protective cases from plants using silk. The larvae primarily consume the invasive duckweed Lemna minuta, a plant known for its rapid growth and negative impacts on ecosystems. C. lemnata is a multivoltine species, with several generations per year, allowing its larvae to feed continuously throughout the year. In later developmental stages, the larvae consume large amounts of plant material, making them effective biocontrol agents. The larvae also use Lemna plants not only for food but to construct floating cases, which protect them from predators and aid buoyancy. This species is a remarkable example of adaptation to aquatic life, as the larvae breathe dissolved oxygen directly through their thin skin. This specimen is about 15-20mm long.

Particularly striking are the orange embryo in the dorsal brood pouch and the greenish digestive tract filled with food particles. Daphnia are among the most common planktonic organisms in freshwater and play a crucial role in aquatic food webs.

description: This species ranges in size from 3–18 centimetres (1.2–7.1 in) and is a burrower, constructing U-shaped holes in the loose substrate near the bases of coral reefs in water ranging from 3–40 metres (9.8–131.2 ft). It's a smasher, with club-shaped raptorial appendages. An agile and active intertidal and sub-intertidal predator, it prefers gastropods, crustaceans, and bivalves, and will repeatedly deliver blunt force to the exoskeleton of its prey until it can gain access to the underlying soft tissue for consumption. It is reported to have a "punch" of over 80 km/h (50 miles/h), the fastest recorded punch of any living animal. The acceleration is similar to that in a .22 LR bullet fired from a handgun.
